title: The house of the Aziz
hookLine: the lady of the house tries to seduce him, and he says: I seek refuge in Allah
last: THE PRICE THEY PAID ISN'T YOUR WORTH.

cards: Temptation rarely arrives when you're weak and alone in a dark alley. More often it shows up when life is going well. The job, the trust, the key to the building.
Nobody's watching. Yusuf has grown up in the house of the man who bought him. The Qur'an calls that man al-Aziz, a title, something like the mighty one, a high official of Egypt.
Yusuf has reached his full strength, and the verse says he's been given wisdom and knowledge. He's trusted, he's handsome, he lives under their roof. And the lady of the house has noticed.

teach.b: Surah Yusuf, verse twenty-three, told with great restraint. She, in whose house he was, tried to turn him from himself. She closed the doors, and said: come.
Yusuf's answer, in Pickthall's old translation: "I seek refuge in Allah!" In Arabic, ma'adha-llah.

teach.h: MY MASTER — THE MAN, OR GOD?
teach.b: Then his reasons: he's my master, he's treated me well; and wrongdoers don't prosper. Who is my master? Commentators split.

Some say the Aziz, who gave him a good home. Others say his Lord, Allah. The Arabic word, rabb, can carry both, and the verse may be holding both at once: loyalty to the man who trusted him, and to the God who made him.
Then a verse commentators read in more than one way: she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the clear sign of his Lord. What was the sign?
The Qur'an doesn't say; commentators have offered many answers. What it does say is that Yusuf was human, the pull was real, and he turned.

His phrase has a close cousin in daily Muslim life: a'udhu billah. The Qur'an tells its readers to seek refuge in Allah before reciting, and Muslims also say it when anger rises, or a bad thought knocks.
Seeking refuge is not proving you're strong. It's admitting you need a place to run to, and running there. Yusuf didn't argue with the temptation, or out-think it.
He named where he was going, and he went.

how: Muslims say a'udhu billah, "I seek refuge in Allah," before reciting the Qur'an, when angry, and when tempted; Yusuf's words in the house of the Aziz are a well-known example.

o: God willing, said of plans for the future
I seek refuge in Allah, said when tempted
praise be to God, said after good news

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an says Yusuf felt no pull at all
it says he would have desired her, had he not seen the clear sign of his Lord.
the Qur'an explains exactly what the sign was
it doesn't. commentators have offered many answers; the text is silent.
Muslims say a'udhu billah before reading the Qur'an
seeking refuge in Allah opens the recitation, and is said when anger or temptation rises.

games.q: you're Yusuf. the doors are closed, nobody is watching, and the lady of the house says: come. what do you say?
games.why: ma'adha-llah: I seek refuge in Allah. then his reasons: my master has treated me well, and wrongdoers don't prosper.

practice: Think of the thing that tempts you most often, maybe small: the extra drink, the cruel comment, the scroll at two in the morning, the lie that would make things easier, and picture it knocking.
Instead of arguing with it, picture turning and walking somewhere safe; if you pray, you can say a'udhu billah, I seek refuge in Allah, and let the words be the door you step through.
If not, choose one word that means safe to you, and practice going there.

wordCard.voice: Ma'adha-llah, I seek refuge in Allah: what Yusuf said when the lady of the house closed the doors behind him.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:23: "I seek refuge in Allah" — a close cousin of a'udhu billah.

carryVoice: Your line: I seek refuge. Short words, for the moment the doors close. That's sixty days.
